### Team Name

Routes@NUS

### Proposed Level of Achievement

Artermis

### Motivation

Whenever we travel to a part of the NUS campus we have not been to before, we often rely on NUSMods Venues to get a general gist of where we are headed. However, we are unsure of how to get there, how long it takes to get there, as well as the optimal path of getting there. It may be confusing to constantly switch between Google maps and NUSMods Venues to find our way, and Google maps often has insufficient information regarding venues indoors (e.g. how to get to programming labs in COM1). Therefore we wish to create a mobile app that serves to bridge

### Aim

We hope to create Routes@NUS, a mobile application that helps users pathfind/navigate from their current position in school (or wherever they select as their starting position) to where they want to go within school with greater precision than Google Maps, in terms of routing as well as time estimates. We also would like to provide indoor floor plan guidance, to allow for greater clarity when navigating the school campus. Our app will also allow users to keep a list of saved locations, for quicker lookup to destinations they frequent.

### User Stories

1. As a NUS student who wants to get to a classroom I am unfamiliar with, I want to be able to find the optimal path to get to my classroom, so that I do not waste time travelling.
2. As a NUS student who is new to campus, I want to search for buildings, classrooms, and common locations by name, so that I can find my destination even if I do not know the exact building code.
3. As a NUS student, I would like to know how long it takes to travel to my desired location reliably (taking into account internal shuttle bus timings) so that I can properly plan my commute.
4. As a NUS student, I want to compare different route options such as fastest route, shortest route, and accessible route, so that I can choose the route that best fits my needs.
5. As a wheelchair bound NUS student, I would like to know what accessible routes are available to get to my desired location so that I do not have to worry about taking an inaccessible path.
6. As a NUS student, I want to be able to quickly access locations I frequently visit, so that I can conveniently check how long it takes to get there from my current location.
7. As a NUS student, I want the app to distinguish between outdoor paths, indoor corridors, stairs, lifts, and shuttle bus segments, so that I understand what type of travel each part of the route involves.

### Scope of Project

Initially proposed to map out the whole of NUS campus, but once delving into the project, we realised how many nodes we may need to set manually in order for backend A-star search algorithm to work correctly and optimally. For now we plan to decrease the scope and map out COM1, COM2, COM3 and take the center of University Town as 1 node. We will continue to map out nodes in school as much as possible and slowly increase the scope. However, we will promise to deliver minimally the whole of Computing by the end of Orbital. We hope that our features are still of standard to be considered for Artermis, despite the smaller scope.

### Feature Overview

Proposed Features:  
Feature 1 (core): Finding the shortest/fastest path to get from Point A to point B within NUS campus \+ estimated distance travelled and walking time  
Feature 2 (core): Map highlighted and colour coded according to mode of travel along that edge  
Feature 3 (core): Generating instructions on how to follow the given path.  
Feature 4 (core): Implement available options of travelling, e.g. walking only, fastest route (walk \+ ride internal shuttle bus), accessible routes  
Feature 5 (core): Implement an “indoor” tab for users to reference, seeing the relevant floor plans they may come across in their route (button available to select which floor they want to see)  
Feature 6 (core): General map that when clicking on specific POIs, can pull up the floor plan of those buildings  
Feature 7 (extension): Favourite/save certain locations for quick access  
Feature 8 (extension): Display a list of recently visited/searched locations  
Feature 9 (extension): Customisation of pacing (as some users may walk faster than others)  
Feature 10:(extension): Display level of congestion on bus to users

Current Features Implemented: (discussed in further detail under **Current Progress**)

1. Fastest route from current location to available locations
2. Generated instructions on how to follow the given path
3. User sign up and log in
4. Saved locations for each user that user can set
5. Limited nodes created (\~40 nodes)

### System Design

For milestone 1, we broke down the project into the frontend and backend and worked on both separately. The app is split into a React Native frontend and a FastAPI backend. The frontend handles user interaction, map display, route confirmation, navigation screens, and saved locations. The backend stores campus map data, users, saved locations, and routing-related information. We used PostgreSQL as our database, with Alembic to handle schema migrations.

### Tech Stack

Frontend: React Native \+ Expo  
Backend: FastAPI  
Database: PostgreSQL / Supabase  
ORM & Migrations: SQLAlchemy \+ Alembic  
External Services: Google Maps API  
Deployment: Render \+ EAS Build

### Frontend

1. React Native: Main framework used, allows us to write one unified codebase that can be deployed for both iOS and Android. For Milestone 1 submission, we will only be building the Android APK for ease of testing.  
   The React Native frontend is organised around screens, reusable components, API calls to backend, and TanStack Query custom hooks.
2. react-native-maps: Library used to render google maps into the app, has diverse features such as Marker, Polyline and Polygon that allow us to manipulate the rendered map to show for example coverage of area, as well as render a route via a list of coordinates.
3. expo-location: Library used to ask for permission to obtain device’s location and therefore its coordinates. Coordinates are being fed to the backend to determine the closest node user should start navigating from.
4. expo-secure-store: Library used by expo apps to encrypt and securely store keys. We will eventually use this feature to store auth bearer tokens in the future, but for now our current login system uses a simple signup and login logic
5. TanStack Query: Library to abstract and manage the states when data is loading, has been loaded or when an error has occurred. Simplifies the API calling process and helps us manage our pages better.

### Backend

1. FastAPI: Backend framework used for routing. Simple and straight forward routes allowing us to quickly set up the backend. We chose a python backend framework as we are both familiar with python and did not want to sink too much time in learning another framework.
2. Database (PostgreSQL): PostgreSQL supports relationship well which helps to connect related data such as map_edges to its from_node_id and to_node_id, preventing invalid data, in addition PostgreSQL works well with SQLAlchemy and FastAPI
3. ORM (SQLAlchemy): Library to map Python model classes such as Location, Map_Node and Map_Edges to PostgreSQL database tables
4. Asyncpg: asyncpg is the asynchronous PostgreSQL driver for SQLAlchemy, which helps the FastAPI backend to perform asynchronous database operations
5. Alembic: Library used to manage database migrations, keeps track of changes to the database schema, such as adding column and modifying constraints, allowing these changes to be applied consistently across different development and deployment environments
6. The backend framework is built on FastAPI, with API format as REST API with JSON

The algorithm employed for routing is A star, heuristic as fastest time to complete route (arbitrarily assumed).

We have built several routers. The key ones are locations, routes, users, saved locations and campus_map each with their API endpoints.

Fastest route from current location to available locations \+  
Generated instructions on how to follow path  
![][image2]  
![][image3]  
Frontend wise, relevant screens needed have been implemented, from the home page (1st screen) user enters a search input, which brings them to the search page (2nd screen) to specify a node we already have in our database. Afterwards, when the destination node is selected, the origin node and destination node are passed to the backend, calling the A-star search algorithm to start from the origin node and find the fastest path to the destination node. As currently we are still in the Ideation phase, we have only implemented the simplest fastest route option. Other options such as walk only, and accessible paths will have to be implemented in the future, where we gather more node data to add to our backend.

Once the routes are done generating in backend (currently only fastest route), all routes will be passed back to frontend and listed as options for users to choose from as seen from the 3rd screen.

Choosing the route will bring users to the 4th screen where they can preview the route and decide if they would like to use this route. Confirming the route brings them to the 5th screen, allowing them to begin their navigation. At the bottom of the 5th screen, there is a modal button that brings up the generated instructions on how to follow the path. The generated instructions are stored within edges from one node to another.

User sign up and log in  
![][image4]  
When the user goes to the settings page and clicks on the account, he will be given the choice to sign up and login. When signing up, username and password will be sent to the backend, checking if there already exists a user with that username. If not, the backend will proceed with creation of users in the Users table. The password will be hashed with a SHA256 function before being stored in the database.  
Similarly for logging in, the password will be hashed before backend checks for a user with the same username and password.  
Saved locations for each user that user can set  
![][image5]  
In saved locations, if the user has logged into their account, the user will be able to start saving locations (a bookmark icon will appear beside destinations).

Upon clicking on the empty bookmark icon, a pop-up window will appear, asking for the purpose of saving this location. Once entered, it will be sent to backend to be stored in a Saved_locations table, can be identified by the user_id and location_id as composite key  
The change is then reflected to the user as a filled in blue bookmark

**Features to be implemented**  
Map highlighted and colour coded according to mode of travel along that edge  
![][image3]  
Currently our routing is one single colour, showing the route from start to end, but we want the map to highlight different parts of a route using different colours depending on the mode of travel, such as walking or shuttle bus.. This helps users quickly understand how they will travel along each section of the route.

We can implement this by having each edge in the route graph store a mode field (which has already been added in the tables). When rendering the route on the map, the frontend can split the route into segments and apply different polyline colours based on the mode of travel. For example, walking paths can be shown in blue, bus routes in green, and indoor paths in orange.

Implement available options of travelling  
Currently when choosing the route and as previously explained, we have only implemented the routing for the fastest path using A-star search. In the future we will implement more route options to be available to users so that users can choose between different route preferences, such as fastest route, shortest walking distance, sheltered route, wheelchair-accessible route, or route with fewer stairs. This makes the app more flexible for different user needs.

We can implement this by having the backend routing algorithm support different weighting strategies. For example, a fastest route can prioritise travel time, while an accessible route can avoid edges marked as stairs or inaccessible. By adjusting the heuristic for A-star, we can develop different route options. In the case for more complex functions such as travelling by car to a carpark, we may have to use the google map API as well.  
Implement an “indoor” tab for users to reference  
Currently, COM1 floorplans have been hardcoded into the demo APK for MS1, but the retrieval of floor plans will need to be dynamic depending on the buildings visited en route.  
We already have building_code as a field in map_nodes, so all that is left is finding the relevant floor plans for buildings in SoC and other locations if possible.

POIs look up in main Map  
We want users to be able to search for points of interest directly from the main map, such as canteens, libraries, bus stops, toilets, study areas, or lecture theatres. This makes the map more useful beyond route planning.

From a set of building locations, we will retrieve their building code and place them as a field in a Marker component that will hold a function to pull up the indoor floor plans of the building_code it has been primed with. This Marker component will be rendered on the main Map, getting its coordinates from the individual building locations.

Display a list of recently visited/searched locations  
We want the home page to display a list of locations that the user recently searched for or navigated to. This allows users to quickly revisit common destinations without searching again.

To implement this, we will probably have to create another table similar to Saved_locations, except that instead of locations to be saved, navigated locations will automatically be pushed to this recently visited table with the user_id and a timestamp for when this location was navigated to. We will limit the number of recently visited locations to be 5 per user, where when another location needs to be added to this table, the oldest entry will be removed.

Customisation of pacing  
We want users to be able to customize their walking speed or pacing so that estimated travel times are more accurate for them. This is useful because different users may walk at different speeds or require more time to move between locations.

A user setting can be added for walking pace, such as slow, normal, or fast. The backend can use this value when calculating walking time along edges. For example, the same walking distance can produce a longer estimated time for users who select a slower pace. This setting can be saved in the user’s profile settings.

Display level of congestion on bus to users  
When we integrate the NUS NextBUS API, we want to display the congestion level of NUS shuttle buses so that users can decide whether they want to wait for the bus or not.

Actually this info is already available in the NUS NextBUS API, but we have yet to receive a reply from the developer team with regards to how to use the NUS NextBUS API, will send a follow up email soon to inquire on this matter.
